links.note: In 388 Theodosius ordered a bishop to rebuild a burned synagogue at Callinicum. Ambrose wrote to him against it. He would not go up to the altar until the emperor promised to drop the case. In 390 came the massacre at Thessalonica. Ambrose then wrote that he dared not offer the sacrifice with Theodosius there.

links.note: Moses of Khoren says the young Nerses, later head of the Armenian church, was then a student at Caesarea in Cappadocia. He also notes that a later head was put in place without the archbishop of Caesarea. That implies earlier heads had been. When Moses himself wrote is disputed, with dates from the fifth to the eighth century.

links.note: John Chrysostom was made bishop of Constantinople. Socrates says it was the emperor's court that chose him. The chamberlain Eutropius told Theophilus of Alexandria to consecrate John or face trial. Back in 381 the emperor had made a law. It named the bishops whose communion marked a Catholic church, and Diodore of Tarsus was one of them.

sources.work: Socrates, Church History VI.2 (trans. Zenos, NPNF 2.2)
sources.quote: The court however gave the preference to John:

links.note: Two synods condemned John Chrysostom. Then the emperor barred him from his own church. Two months later, as Socrates writes, 'a decree of the emperor sent him into exile'.

links.note: In 553 a council at Constantinople condemned Theodore of Mopsuestia by name. He had been dead for more than a hundred years. Its twelfth canon curses anyone who defends him or says his reading of Scripture is orthodox.

sources.work: Second Council of Constantinople (553), Capitulum XII (NPNF 2.14)

links.note: Barhadbeshabba wrote about the year 600. He says Theodore's commentaries were put into Syriac at Edessa, where future Persian bishops studied them. In 585 a synod of the Church of the East spoke up for 'the books and the teaching of saint Theodore' against those who attacked him.

links.note: Calvin's Institutes quote Chrysostom with delight: 'The foundation of our philosophy is humility.' Yet Calvin also faults him and the other Greek Fathers. He says they gave the human will too much power.

links.note: The Augsburg Confession of 1530 calls on Chrysostom as a witness to how the early church shared Communion. Melanchthon wrote a defense of the Confession, known as the Apology. In it he quotes a saying of Chrysostom. It runs: contrition in the heart, confession in the mouth, humility in the work.

sources.work: Augsburg Confession, Article XXIV (Of the Mass) (Project Gutenberg English text)
sources.quote: Chrysostom says that the priest stands daily at the altar, inviting some to the Communion and keeping back others.

sources.quote: Likewise Chrysostom says: In the heart, contrition; in the mouth, confession; in the work, entire humility.

links.note: The Council of Aquileia met in 381. There the city's own bishop, Valerian, spoke out against Palladius, who was a Homoian bishop. He said that whoever defends Arius is an Arian. And whoever will not condemn the blasphemies of Arius, he added, is a blasphemer as well. The council condemned both Palladius and Secundianus.

links.note: At Aquileia in 381, Ambrose led the questioning of Palladius, a Homoian bishop. Palladius would not condemn a letter of Arius, so Ambrose had it read out. In Milan in 386 he preached against Auxentius, a rival bishop who was also Homoian. He declared him cast out.

links.note: In 416 or 417, Jerome's monasteries at Bethlehem were attacked and burned, and his deacon was killed. Augustine wrote that followers of Pelagius were said to have done it. Pope Innocent noted that the women who told him of it had not named the man behind it, though he saw no doubt about who was guilty. So the charge rests on report, not on a named act.

sources.work: Augustine, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, chapter 66
sources.quote: Certain followers of Pelagius are said to have carried their support of his cause after these judicial proceedings to an incredible extent of perverseness and audacity.

links.note: In 1546 the Council of Trent ruled that the old Latin Vulgate was authentic. It was to be the text for public reading and preaching. Its English translator of 1848 says the council chose the Vulgate as Jerome's version. Augustine had said Jerome's work was a translation from the Hebrew.

links.note: Gennadius of Marseilles wrote about Rufinus around 480. He calls him a priest of the church at Aquileia. Rufinus, he says, opened up much Greek writing to Latin readers. Among the works that Rufinus put into Latin, he lists books by Basil of Caesarea and by Gregory of Nazianzus as well.

sources.work: Gennadius, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 17 (Rufinus)
sources.quote: translating the works of Basil of Cæsarea in Cappadocia, Gregory Nazianzan, that most eloquent man,

links.note: Gregory of Tours wrote in the late sixth century. He tells how a light from Hilary's church at Poitiers shone over King Clovis as he marched against the Arian Visigoths. Gregory saw it as Hilary's help against 'those heretics' he had once fought. He calls Hilary a defender of the Trinity who was sent into exile for its sake.

sources.work: Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks II.37
sources.quote: it signified that aided by the light of the blessed confessor Hilary he might more surely overcome the host of those heretics against whom the saint himself had so often done battle for the faith.

sources.work: Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks III, preface
sources.quote: Hilary, blessed defender of the undivided Trinity, and for its sake driven into exile,* was both restored to his own country and entered Paradise.

links.note: In 535 the emperor Justinian made a law for Africa, which his armies had won back. It named the Donatists along with Arians, Jews and pagans, and barred them from holding services. In the 590s Pope Gregory the Great wrote to the emperor Maurice. He praised the orders Maurice had given against the Donatists.

sources.work: Justinian, Novel 37 (to Solomon, praetorian prefect of Africa, 1 August 535)
sources.quote: Neque enim Iudaeos neque paganos neque Donatistas neque Árianos neque alios quoscumque haereticos vel speluncas habere vel quaedam quasi ritu ecclesiastico facere patimur,

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Register VI.65 (NPNF numbering), to the Emperor Mauricius
sources.quote: Now after what manner the serenity of your Piety, out of regard to righteousness and zeal for the purest religion, has been moved against the most flagitious pravity of the Donatists, the tenor of the commands which you have sent most clearly shews.

links.from_name: The Roman Church in the Age of Gregory the Great
links.note: Pope Gregory the Great wrote to Columbus, a Numidian bishop, in the early 590s. He had heard that the Donatists were spreading and baptizing many people a second time. He ordered a council of bishops to look into it.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Register II.48 (NPNF numbering), to Columbus, bishop
sources.quote: the heresy of the Donatists is for our sins spreading daily, and that very many, leave being given them through venality, are being baptized a second time by the Donatists.

links.note: Sulpicius Severus says Spanish bishops got an order from the emperor Gratian that drove the heretics out. Later Maximus, who had seized the throne, heard the case at Trier. He decreed that Priscillian and his friends be put to death.

sources.work: Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History II.47
sources.quote: a rescript was, on the entreaty of Ydacius, obtained from Gratianus, who was then emperor,

sources.work: Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History II.50
sources.quote: the emperor decreed that Priscillian and his friends should be put to death.

links.note: Sulpicius Severus says Priscillian and two bishops went to Rome and Milan around 382 to clear their names. Damasus of Rome would not see them. At Milan they found Ambrose just as opposed.

sources.work: Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History II.48
sources.quote: Returning to Milan, they found that Ambrose was equally opposed to them.

sources.work: Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History II.48
sources.quote: When they reached Rome with the wish of clearing themselves before Damasus, they were not even admitted to his presence.

links.note: Martin of Tours was at the emperor Maximus's court at Trier during the Priscillian affair. Sulpicius Severus says he begged Maximus not to shed the blood of the accused. He called it an unheard-of outrage for a secular ruler to judge a church case.

sources.work: Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History II.50
sources.quote: For Martin, being then settled at Treves, did not cease to importune Ithacius, that he should give up his accusations, or to implore Maximus that he should not shed the blood of the unhappy persons in question.

sources.work: Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History II.50
sources.quote: it was, besides, a foul and unheard-of indignity, that a secular ruler should be judge in an ecclesiastical cause.

links.note: The emperor Constantius II called the bishops to two councils in 359. He hoped to bring them all to one creed. A council at Constantinople in 360 confirmed the creed read at Ariminum, and Ulfila of the Goths signed it. In 427 or 428 the Homoian bishop Maximinus still named that creed as his faith.

links.note: Jerome wrote his Dialogue against the Luciferians in about 379. In it he blames the Homoian leaders Valens and Ursacius for what was done at the council of Ariminum. There, he says, the Nicene faith was condemned, and the whole world groaned to find itself Arian.

links.note: Theodoret, who wrote in the fifth century, says Bishop Leontius of Antioch made Aetius a deacon. Two ascetics of the city, Flavian and Diodore, protested in public that this brought shame on the church. Leontius then suspended Aetius.

sources.work: Theodoret, Church History II.19 (trans. Jackson, NPNF 2.3)
sources.quote: At this juncture Aetius, the master of Eunomius, who promoted the Arian error by his speculations, was admitted to the diaconate.

sources.work: Theodoret, Church History II.19 (trans. Jackson, NPNF 2.3)
sources.quote: Flavianus and Diodorus, however, who had embraced an ascetic career, and were open champions of the Apostolic decrees, publicly protested against the attacks of Leontius against true religion.

sources.work: Theodoret, Church History II.19 (trans. Jackson, NPNF 2.3)
sources.quote: That a man nurtured in iniquity and scheming to win notoriety by ungodliness should be counted worthy of the diaconate, was, they urged, a disgrace to the Church.
